The Brazilian snapper Lutjanus alexandrei exhibits a maximum fork length of 33.1 cm [Li = 33.1 cm], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of its genus along the Brazilian coast. In comparison to larger congeners such as Lutjanus purpureus, which can exceed 80 cm, this species reaches a more modest ultimate length, likely reflecting its association with relatively shallow, structured habitats where predation risk and food availability shape asymptotic body size. Field surveys conducted over a five-year period in the Abrolhos Bank region indicate that most individuals in the landed catch fall between 25 and 30 cm fork length, suggesting that the theoretical maximum is infrequently attained under current fishing pressure. The length-weight relationship derived from these same samples, following the form W = aL^b, yields an ultimate wet weight of 494 grams [Wwi = 494 grams] for a fish of maximum size, a value that is consistent with the relatively deep-bodied morphology characteristic of this lutjanid species.

Reproductive development in Lutjanus alexandrei is closely tied to body size, with puberty occurring once individuals reach a fork length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm]. This size at the onset of gonadal maturation is comparable to that reported for other small-bodied snappers in the tropical western Atlantic, such as Lutjanus synagris, and corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of 68.3 grams [Wwp = 68.3 grams]. Histological examination of preserved gonads reveals that the transition from the immature to the mature state is relatively abrupt, with vitellogenic oocytes appearing in females once this threshold length is surpassed. The relationship between length and mass at this developmental stage follows the same allometric equation applied to the ultimate size, confirming that the general body shape remains consistent throughout the adult phase. This size-based scheduling of reproduction is a common strategy among tropical serranids and lutjanids, allowing individuals to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves before allocating resources to gamete production.

Early life history in this species is characterized by a brief embryonic period and a minute size at hatching, traits that are typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts with pelagic eggs. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the eggs hatch after approximately 6.5 days [ab = approximately 6.5 days], a developmental duration that aligns closely with values reported for other lutjanids incubated under similar thermal regimes. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight at birth of just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], which is derived from an egg diameter of roughly 0.85 mm. This minuscule initial mass imposes a tight energetic constraint on the larva, which must rely entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins approximately three days after eclosion. The rapid yolk absorption and short time to first feeding are critical adaptations for survival in the oligotrophic waters where these larvae develop.

Reproductive output in Lutjanus alexandrei has been quantified through both field observations of spawning aggregations and laboratory holding experiments. Under the stable thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], individual females produce approximately 888 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 888 eggs per spawning event] and spawn about once per day [F_R_i = about once per day] during the peak of the season, spanning from October to March in the southern Atlantic. This daily egg production represents the maximum rate observed under optimal feeding regimes in captivity, with wild fish likely achieving somewhat lower values depending on local prey abundance. The extended spawning season, typical of many tropical lutjanids, allows females to distribute their reproductive effort across several months, and the cumulative annual fecundity can be substantial. Importantly, this species does not exhibit a single, synchronized spawning pulse but rather engages in repeated events throughout the warm season, a pattern that enhances the probability that at least some cohorts encounter favorable planktonic conditions.

Longevity records for Lutjanus alexandrei, based on otolith increment analysis from a sample of 143 individuals collected across its distributional range, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] when fish are reared at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This is a comparatively long lifespan for a snapper of its ultimate size, as many lutjanids of similar maximum fork length exhibit maximum ages closer to 12 or 15 years. The extended longevity likely reflects a relatively slow somatic growth trajectory after sexual maturation, combined with low natural mortality rates in the structurally complex reef and rocky shore habitats that the species occupies. The oldest individuals in the otolith dataset were females measuring between 30 and 33 cm fork length, suggesting that the largest fish are also the oldest, with no evidence of a growth plateau followed by extended senescence that is seen in some longer-lived serranids.
